Noble
NOH-bul
adj. / n.
Latin nobilis, well-known, high-born, from noscere, to know—originally the family everyone knows. The KJV keeps both the birth sense and the character sense, and Acts 17 quietly transfers the honor from the first to the second.

Biblical Definition

Noble in the KJV first means high-born or high-ranked, and Scripture is candid that such men are rarely the ones God calls: ye see your calling, brethren, how that not many wise men after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called (1 Cor 1:26). The kingdom does not recruit from the top of the social register. But the word's most important use redefines nobility outright. Luke says of the Jews at Berea, These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so (Acts 17:11). Their nobility had nothing to do with birth, wealth or rank. It consisted of two things: an open readiness to hear, and a daily labor of checking what they heard against Scripture—even when the preacher was the apostle Paul. Teachability and verification, together, are what Scripture calls noble. Isaiah supplies the Old Testament parallel in a verse about generosity of soul: the liberal deviseth liberal things; and by liberal things shall he stand (Isa 32:8), where the noble man is marked by what he plans for others. Nehemiah records the counterexample—nobles who would not put their necks to the work of the Lord while everyone else built the wall. Rank without labor is not nobility in Scripture; it is an indictment.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines NOBLE as great, elevated, dignified; illustrious; exalted in rank or excellence of character; magnanimous; and as a noun, a person of rank above a commoner.

expand to see more

NOBLE, a. — Great; elevated; dignified; being above every thing that can dishonor reputation; as a noble mind; a noble courage.

NOBLE, a. — Of an ancient and splendid family; of high rank in society. Also, magnanimous; generous; liberal; as a noble heart.

NOBLE, n. — A person of rank above a commoner; a nobleman.

Key Scripture

Acts 17:11 — "These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so."

1 Corinthians 1:26 — "For ye see your calling, brethren, how that not many wise men after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called:"

Isaiah 32:8 — "But the liberal deviseth liberal things; and by liberal things shall he stand."

Modern Corruption

Nobility now attaches to visibility—celebrity, platform, or the right public opinions—while Acts 17 assigns it to two unglamorous habits: a mind ready to receive, and daily verification of what it is told against Scripture.

expand to see more

The modern aristocracy is one of attention. Fame confers moral standing; a large audience is treated as evidence of worth, and public alignment with the correct position substitutes for character. Scripture's test is stubbornly private and repetitive. The Bereans were called noble for reading, daily, with an open mind and a checking pen, and no one would have known they were doing it. There is no way to perform Berean nobility for an audience, which is exactly why it is worth something.

The second corruption runs inside the church: nobility of soul confused with agreeableness. Being more noble in Acts 17 involved verifying an apostle's preaching against the text—an act that looks, from the platform, like insufficient trust. Luke commends it without qualification. And Nehemiah's nobles are a permanent warning in the other direction: men of rank who would not put their necks to the work while the goldsmiths and merchants built. Rank that will not labor is not nobility but its counterfeit.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew nadib, willing, generous, noble—a word about a liberal spirit before it is about rank; Greek eugenēs, well-born, used comparatively of the Bereans.

expand to see more

Hebrew nadib (H5081) — noble, willing, generous; rooted in a verb meaning to volunteer, so nobility is first a freely offered spirit (Exod 35:5; 1 Sam 2:8; Isa 32:8).

Hebrew chor (H2715) — a noble, one free-born; Nehemiah's nobles who would not work (Neh 3:5; 6:17; Jer 27:20).

Greek eugenēs (G2104) — well-born, high in rank, and by extension noble-minded; more noble than those in Thessalonica (Luke 19:12; Acts 17:11; 1 Cor 1:26).

Usage

"More noble... in that they received the word... and searched the scriptures daily—the biblical test."

"Not many noble are called—the kingdom does not recruit from the top of the register."

"Nehemiah's nobles would not put their necks to the work; rank that will not labor is a counterfeit."
